prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, from magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms to many-atom clock operation at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock (B052) as a single-part prize to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. The chair asked me to say what in the record makes Ye's role original and decisive and not an improvement of Katori's invention. Having gone through what I know, I think the answer is yes, with a caveat about verification. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock, and that is the invention. But the clock only became what the committee would be crediting through a second line of original experiments that came mainly out of the JILA group under Ye: the sub-hertz and then roughly one-second optical coherence in a lattice, the systematic evaluations that took uncertainty from the 10^-16 range to the low 10^-18 range, the demonstration that collisions and many-body interactions in a degenerate gas can be controlled and used (spin-exchange and Pauli-blocking effects, the three-dimensional lattice clock), and later the differential comparison inside one sample that resolves gravitational redshift over about a millimetre. Johansson's division of the credit (concept and first demonstration versus ultimate performance and many-body operation) is the right way to word it, and it is a division between two kinds of original work, not between a discoverer and a follower. Ye also worked with Katori and Kimble on the state-insensitive trap idea in the same period. I cannot verify exact dates and first-author attributions from this record, so I ask the secretariat to check them before the final vote, but I no longer think Ye's credit is the weak point. The remaining ingredients are what I look for: an invention that opens a door to something we could not see, independent verification in several national laboratories, and a short, clear credit list.
statement.case_against: My reservations are smaller than in round 1 but not gone. First, the statutes ask for the original experiment, and a two-name list inevitably leaves out real claimants: Lemonde and the SYRTE group, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Takamoto, and the Yb, Hg and Al+ groups. I accept that Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and others did much of the day-to-day work at JILA, but that is the usual relation between a laboratory head and the people in it, and it does not change who the originators are in a prize sense. Second, the overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize is a real wording risk. I accept the argument that the comb is a ruler and the lattice clock is a new reference oscillator, but the citation must name the lattice clock and say what is new, not speak of precision spectroscopy in general. Third, several fundamental-physics payoffs (constants, dark matter) are still prospective, so the committee should not lean on them in the citation. I do not regard the pending redefinition of the second as a criterion and would not use it either way.

responses.point: The credit splits along an easy distinction: the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice demonstration are Katori's, while the push to the lowest systematic uncertainty, long coherence and Fermi-degenerate operation is Ye's. The citation should name the lattice clock specifically.
responses.response: This is the most useful answer to the chair's question and I rely on it, since you know the field better than I do. It persuades me because it describes two different kinds of original work, not a first and an improved version of the same thing: a concept with a first demonstration, and a regime (many-atom, quantum-degenerate, 10^-18) that nobody expected to be reachable and that took distinct experimental ideas to reach. I withdraw my phrase 'improving a technique' as the description of Ye's role. I still ask you to confirm which of the many-body and degenerate-gas results were first achieved in Ye's laboratory, because the committee record should state this and not leave it as a general impression. I agree with you that tradition and the SI second should not be arguments for the prize.

responses.point: The comb is a ruler and the lattice clock is a new reference oscillator with its own physics (magic-wavelength trapping, many-atom interrogation, control of blackbody and collisional shifts), so the 2005 prize does not exhaust it, and the citation should be worded around the lattice clock itself.
responses.response: I accept this and it answers the question I put to you in round 1, which was whether the overlap is argued from the record or from impression. You argue it from what is physically new, which is what I wanted. I would add two items to the wording. The citation should name magic-wavelength trapping and many-atom interrogation, so a reader sees at once the difference from the comb and the ion clock, and it should not use 'precision spectroscopy' or 'metrology' alone. My draft citation does this. I also note you and Kroll said your near-identical openings are not independent evidence, so I rest on the physics you describe and not on the agreement.

responses.point: Katori's and Ye's contributions are of different kinds (concept and first demonstration versus ultimate performance), so the citation must be worded to avoid implying that one of them merely refined the other. Credit also goes beyond three names, including SYRTE, Ludlow, Takamoto and the Yb and Hg groups.
responses.response: I agree on both and the wording matters because that was my own worry. My answer to the second point is that the long list of other contributors is an argument for a citation that is narrow and exact, not for widening the list: the prize may name at most three people, and Katori and Ye are the two on whom the invention and the decisive demonstration rest, while the independent SYRTE, PTB, NIST and RIKEN comparisons are what establish verification, not rival priority. I would ask the secretariat to note in the record that the SYRTE and Yb and Hg groups are acknowledged as independent contributors. I would not add Lemonde as a third name without a priority argument that I have not seen; if anyone has one, I want to hear it before the vote, because it is the only change to the configuration that I could accept.

responses.point: Twisted bilayer graphene (B024) is a simple mechanism confirmed by nature, the existence of flat-band correlated phases does not depend on the unresolved pairing mechanism, and Mehlig says he would not treat the choice as lopsided.
responses.response: I take the distinction between unsettled interpretation and unsettled discovery seriously, and I agree that the correlated phases are reproduced, which my round-1 reply did not give enough weight to. It does not change my position this year, because for me the deciding issue is the credit list and not the physics. Cao as first author of the 2018 experiments, the earlier Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto theory, and the other groups that reproduced the phases are outside the three names, and I cannot tell the committee with confidence which people did the original work. B052 has the opposite property: two names that nobody has seriously contested. If the committee wishes to return to B024, I would want the attribution question settled first, and I do not think waiting widens it in the way you say, because the early experiments and papers are already well documented.

responses.point: The chair asked that B052 be tested with the atomic-physics members and not rely on a non-specialist reading, and that the question of a nuclear-clock recognition for Ye be kept separate from this prize.
responses.response: I am not an atomic physicist either, so I agree the test belongs with Johansson and Lindroth, and I have asked for the priority points to be checked and not assumed. On the nuclear clock, I think the citation restriction you describe is enough: a prize for the lattice clock says nothing about thorium-229, and a future committee could judge that work on its own merits. It is not a reason to delay. I also note your point that source associations in B043 are still based on a few objects, which is the same maturity concern I have, and why I keep IceCube as an alternative and not as a second part.

uncertainties: Exact priority dates and first-author attributions in the lattice-clock literature. I rely on memory for the JILA coherence, systematic-evaluation and many-body results, and ask that Ye's separate contributions be checked against the published record before the vote.
Whether any priority argument for a third name (for example Lemonde and the SYRTE group) is strong enough to change a two-name credit; I have not seen one.
Whether the citation wording can name the lattice clock and magic-wavelength trapping clearly enough to avoid both the 2005 comb prize and a future nuclear-clock recognition.

Whether the committee regards aberration-corrected electron microscopy (B011) as a discovery or an enabling instrument, and whether Krivanek and the STEM correctors weaken the Rose, Haider and Urban attribution; I cannot settle this from my own position.
How much of the fundamental-physics reach (constants, dark matter) will be demonstrated and not only prospective.
statement.conflict_note: B011 (aberration-corrected electron microscopy) lies in my own research field, transmission electron microscopy, and I am President of the International Federation of Societies for Microscopy, so I would recuse myself from the vote on B011 if it became live and ask colleagues to weigh my earlier advocacy accordingly. I am no longer advancing it as a preferred part this year and keep it only as an alternative. I have no personal tie to Katori, Ye or any credited name on B052 or B043. Goran Johansson is a colleague in Chalmers Physics and Bernhard Mehlig is in the neighbouring Gothenburg department; these are institutional links only and do not affect B052.
